about: The scripted AI lesson for p4-nuclear-fission (2026-11-27, Phase C, brief docs/briefs/2026-11-27-phase-c-physics.md): every word she sees is written here once and checked (tools/check-script.js, tools/review-lesson.js --script). The AI only marks her typed answers (choosing a branch written here), answers her own questions, and sorts her messages. It opens with two recall questions from p4-nuclear-model and p4-radioactivity.

steps.text: Welcome! This lesson is about splitting a nucleus and joining nuclei together: two ways to release huge amounts of energy stored in the nucleus.

steps.question: First, two quick questions from earlier lessons. What charge does a neutron have?
steps.right: Yes: a neutron has no charge.

wrong.positive: Not quite: protons are positive. A neutron has no charge.
wrong.negative: Not quite: electrons are negative. A neutron has no charge.

idk.hint: Protons are positive and electrons are negative. The third particle is neither.

steps.question: Second: what are gamma rays?
steps.right: Yes: gamma rays are electromagnetic radiation, like light but with far more energy.

wrong.other: Not quite: electromagnetic radiation from a nucleus.
wrong.beta: Not quite: fast electrons are beta particles. Gamma rays are electromagnetic radiation from a nucleus.
wrong.alpha: Not quite: helium nuclei are alpha particles. Gamma rays are electromagnetic radiation from a nucleus.

idk.hint: Gamma rays have no mass and no charge: they are waves, not particles. Electromagnetic radiation is waves.

steps.answerWhy: Gamma rays are electromagnetic radiation given out by a nucleus.

steps.text: Now this lesson. An unstable nucleus is one that is likely to change or break apart. Some very large nuclei are unstable.
Remember: the mass number counts protons plus neutrons.
Uranium-235, or U-235, is uranium with mass number 235: one of the isotopes of uranium. Its large nucleus is unstable.
Splitting a large, unstable nucleus into two smaller nuclei is called nuclear fission.

steps.question: In fission, how do the two smaller nuclei compare with each other?

options.text: They are roughly equal in size
One is far bigger than the other
One of them is a single proton

steps.right: Yes: the two smaller nuclei are roughly equal in size.

wrong.other: Not quite: they are roughly equal in size.
wrong.unequal: Not quite: the nucleus splits roughly down the middle: the two smaller nuclei are roughly equal in size.
wrong.proton: Not quite: a single proton is not a nucleus split in two. The two smaller nuclei are roughly equal in size.

idk.hint: Fission splits the nucleus roughly in half.

steps.answerWhy: In fission the two smaller nuclei are roughly equal in size.

steps.text: A nucleus can split on its own, but that is rare. Usually it must first absorb a neutron: the neutron is taken into the nucleus, which makes it even more unstable, and then it splits.
As the nucleus splits, it gives out 2 or 3 neutrons and gamma rays, and a large amount of energy is released.

steps.question: Why do the 2 or 3 neutrons from one fission matter?

options.text: They can make more nuclei split

steps.right: Yes: each can be absorbed by another nucleus and make it split. The next key point is about this.

wrong.other: Not quite: they can make more nuclei split.
wrong.stop: Not quite: free neutrons do the opposite: each can be absorbed by another nucleus and make it split.
wrong.gamma: Not quite: neutrons stay neutrons. Each can be absorbed by another nucleus and make it split.

idk.hint: A nucleus usually splits after it absorbs a neutron. Now there are 2 or 3 new ones.

steps.answerWhy: Each of those neutrons can be absorbed by another nucleus and make it split.

steps.text: The two smaller nuclei and the neutrons are the fission products. They all fly apart fast: they all have kinetic energy.
The picture shows the start of one fission and the particles that fly out. The gamma rays and energy given out are not drawn.
A fuel is a material that stores energy that can be released: by burning or, in a reactor, by fission.
The most common nuclear fuels are uranium-235 and plutonium-239, an isotope of the element plutonium. Both split easily after absorbing a neutron.

steps.prompt: In one line: what happens in nuclear fission?
points: a large unstable nucleus absorbs a neutron
it splits into two smaller nuclei
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: in nuclear fission, a large unstable nucleus absorbs a neutron and splits into two smaller nuclei.

steps.text: One fission leading to more fissions, again and again, is called a chain reaction.

steps.question: One fission gives out 3 neutrons, and each causes a new fission: that is 3 fissions in the second step. If each of those causes 3 more, how many fissions are in the step after that?

wrong.other: Not quite: 9. Each of the 3 fissions causes 3 more: 3 × 3 = 9.
wrong.add: Not quite: 9. Each of the 3 fissions causes 3 more, so multiply: 3 × 3 = 9.
wrong.same: Not quite: 9. Each of the 3 fissions causes 3 more: 3 × 3 = 9.
wrong.next: Not quite: 9. 27 is one step later. Each of the 3 fissions causes 3 more, so the next step has 3 × 3 = 9.
wrong.total: Not quite: 9. 13 is the total so far (1 + 3 + 9). The question asks for that one step: 3 × 3 = 9.

idk.hint: Each of the 3 fissions causes 3 more. Work out 3 × 3.

steps.answerWhy: Each of the 3 fissions causes 3 more, so the next step has 3 × 3 = 9 fissions.

steps.text: If nothing controls a chain reaction, the number of fissions grows very fast, and a huge amount of energy is released almost at once. The explosion of a nuclear weapon comes from this uncontrolled chain reaction.
A nuclear reactor is the part of a nuclear power station where fission happens, with the chain reaction kept under control.
In a reactor, materials that do not split absorb some of the neutrons. Those neutrons cannot go on to cause fissions.
On average, one neutron from each fission goes on to cause just one more. The energy is released at a steady rate: this is a controlled chain reaction.
The picture shows both kinds: an uncontrolled chain reaction that grows, and a controlled one that stays steady.

steps.question: In a reactor, the materials that absorb neutrons start taking in fewer than usual. What happens to the rate at which energy is released?
steps.right: Yes: more neutrons are left to split uranium nuclei, so energy is released faster. That is why the materials must keep absorbing them.

wrong.same: Not quite: more neutrons are left free to split uranium nuclei, so there are more fissions each second and the energy is released faster.
wrong.falls: Not quite: the neutrons those materials take in cannot cause fissions. Fewer taken in leaves more free to split uranium, so the energy is released faster.

idk.hint: Neutrons taken in by those materials cannot cause fissions. With fewer taken in, more are free to split uranium nuclei.

steps.answerWhy: With fewer neutrons absorbed by the control materials, more go on to split uranium, so the energy is released faster.

steps.prompt: In one line: what is the difference between a reactor and a nuclear weapon?
points: in a reactor the chain reaction is controlled
in a weapon the chain reaction is uncontrolled
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: in a reactor the chain reaction is controlled, so energy comes out steadily; in a nuclear weapon it is uncontrolled.

steps.text: Now the opposite of splitting: joining light nuclei. A light nucleus is one with a small mass: only a few protons and neutrons. It has nothing to do with light you can see.
Joining two light nuclei together to form a heavier nucleus is called nuclear fusion.

steps.question: Hydrogen has the lightest nucleus of all. Which of these could be a fusion reaction?

options.text: A uranium nucleus becomes two smaller nuclei
A radium nucleus gives out an alpha particle
Two hydrogen nuclei become one helium nucleus

steps.right: Yes: two light hydrogen nuclei join into a heavier helium nucleus.

wrong.other: Not quite: two hydrogen nuclei become one helium nucleus.
wrong.fission: Not quite: one nucleus becoming two is fission. Fusion is light nuclei joining, such as two hydrogen nuclei becoming a helium nucleus.
wrong.alpha: Not quite: that is radioactive decay. Fusion is light nuclei joining, such as two hydrogen nuclei becoming a helium nucleus.

idk.hint: Fusion takes two light nuclei and makes one heavier nucleus.

steps.answerWhy: Two hydrogen nuclei joining into a helium nucleus is fusion.

steps.text: In fusion, the heavier nucleus has a little less mass than the two light nuclei had added together. That missing mass has become energy, given out as radiation. A tiny amount of mass makes a huge amount of energy.
The picture shows two light nuclei joining into a heavier nucleus, with energy released.
Fusion is the energy source of stars, including the Sun.
Scientists are trying to use fusion to generate electricity, but it has not yet been done on a large scale.

steps.question: Which of these is powered by nuclear fusion?
steps.right: Yes: the Sun, like every star, is powered by fusion.

wrong.power: Not quite: power stations today use fission. The Sun, like every star, is powered by fusion.
wrong.coal: Not quite: coal is burned: a chemical change, not a nuclear one. The Sun is powered by fusion.

idk.hint: Fusion is the energy source of the stars.

steps.answerWhy: Stars, including the Sun, are powered by nuclear fusion.

steps.prompt: In one line: where does the energy released in fusion come from?
points: some of the mass of the nuclei is turned into energy
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: in nuclear fusion, some of the mass of the light nuclei is turned into energy, given out as radiation.

steps.text: Fission and fusion are both nuclear reactions: they change nuclei. Now compare them.

steps.prompt: In one line: how are fission and fusion different?
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: fission splits one large nucleus into two smaller ones, while fusion joins two light nuclei into a heavier one.

steps.question: Which is true of both fission and fusion?

options.text: Both release a large amount of energy
Both are used in power stations today

steps.right: Yes: both are nuclear reactions that release a large amount of energy.

wrong.other: Not quite: both release a large amount of energy.
wrong.split: Not quite: only fission splits a nucleus; fusion joins nuclei. What they share is that both release a large amount of energy.
wrong.power: Not quite: only fission is used in power stations today. What they share is that both release a large amount of energy.

idk.hint: One of them splits nuclei and the other joins them, so the answer is not about splitting. Think about what both give out.

steps.answerWhy: Fission and fusion both change nuclei and both release a large amount of energy.

steps.text: Now for a short quiz: six questions on the whole lesson. Take your time.

steps.question: Quiz, question 1 of 6: in fission, what does the nucleus split into?

options.text: Two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size

steps.right: Yes: two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size.

wrong.other: Not quite: two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size.
wrong.w1: Not quite: it splits into two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size.
wrong.w2: Not quite: it splits into two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size.

steps.answerWhy: In fission a large nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size.

steps.question: Quiz, question 2 of 6: how many neutrons does each fission give out?

wrong.w1: Not quite: each fission gives out 2 or 3 neutrons, which can cause more fissions.
wrong.w2: Not quite: each fission gives out 2 or 3 neutrons.

steps.answerWhy: Each fission gives out 2 or 3 neutrons.

steps.question: Quiz, question 3 of 6: what does an uncontrolled chain reaction cause?

options.text: The explosion of a nuclear weapon

steps.right: Yes: the number of fissions grows so fast that the energy comes out all at once.

wrong.other: Not quite: the explosion of a nuclear weapon.
wrong.w1: Not quite: that is a controlled chain reaction, in a reactor. An uncontrolled one is a nuclear weapon's explosion.
wrong.w2: Not quite: fusion is joining nuclei, a different reaction. An uncontrolled chain reaction is a nuclear weapon's explosion.

steps.answerWhy: The explosion of a nuclear weapon comes from an uncontrolled chain reaction.

steps.question: Quiz, question 4 of 6: which is a fuel for nuclear fission?

wrong.w1: Not quite: coal is burned, a chemical change. Fission splits nuclei of uranium-235 or plutonium-239.
wrong.w2: Not quite: hydrogen has light nuclei, which are joined in fusion. Fission uses uranium-235 or plutonium-239.

steps.answerWhy: The common fission fuels are uranium-235 and plutonium-239.

steps.question: Quiz, question 5 of 6: how does a reactor keep its chain reaction steady?

options.text: Materials absorb some of the neutrons

steps.right: Yes: absorbing some neutrons means each fission causes, on average, one more.

wrong.other: Not quite: materials absorb some of the neutrons.
wrong.w1: Not quite: temperature is not how it is controlled. Materials that do not split absorb some of the neutrons.
wrong.w2: Not quite: that keeps people safe but does not control the reaction. Materials absorb some of the neutrons.

steps.answerWhy: In a reactor, materials that do not split absorb some neutrons, so on average each fission causes just one more.

steps.question: Quiz, question 6 of 6: what usually starts a uranium-235 nucleus splitting?

options.text: It gives out a gamma ray

steps.right: Yes: the nucleus absorbs a neutron, then splits.

wrong.other: Not quite: it absorbs a neutron.
wrong.w1: Not quite: heating does not split a nucleus. It usually splits after it absorbs a neutron.
wrong.w2: Not quite: gamma rays come out during fission; they do not start it. It usually splits after it absorbs a neutron.

steps.answerWhy: A uranium-235 nucleus usually splits after it absorbs a neutron.

steps.text: That's the end of the quiz: you got {right} out of {n}.
